newsitem.title: CANADA: Weak employment growth haunts Canadian economy.
newsitem.headline: Weak employment growth haunts Canadian economy.

text.p: Weak employment numbers will continue to haunt Canada's economy, undermining income growth and leaving household balance sheets vulnerable, said a report on Tuesday by a Canadian economic institute.
The Conference Board of Canada predicted in its spring 1997 outlook that Canada's economy would grow by 2.9 percent in 1997 and 2.7 percent in 1998.
Those forecasts were unchanged from the board's winter outlook.
The poor employment performance was the most disappointing aspect of recent economic data, the board said.

"The most significant change from the previous outlook is the weaker 1997 employment growth down from 2.1 percent in our winter forecast to 1.3 percent in the current forecast," said Jim Frank, the board's vice-president and chief economist.
Canada's unemployment rate now sits at 9.3 percent.
With unemployment remaining above 9.0 percent for the immediate future, the Canadian consumer would likely continue to experience weak income growth, the board said.

Although current economic growth was being led by the export sector, the board said Canada's trade outlook was in danger due to "severe retrenchment in office equipment exports and a sharp rise in machinery and equipment imports."
Further complicating the outlook was possible monetary tightening by the Bank of Canada, which would squeeze indebted Canadian households.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points on March 25. Since then, economists have speculated that U.S. inflation would lead to another Fed hike in May.

"If Canada has to follow, the result would be a sharp drop in consumer spending as household borrowing slows down and the wealth loss from a stock market decline hits consumer balance sheets," Frank said.
